sentences: On a snow-covered hillside, one pine stands bolt upright while a second, its roots laid bare, leans across in front of it.
This is Snow-Covered Pines, painted in ink on paper by the eighteenth-century scholar-painter Yi In-sang.
Yi In-sang, known by his pen name Neunghogwan, lived from 1710 to 1760.
He was born into a branch of a noble family barred from high office.
He rose no higher than magistrate of Eumjuk County, yet he was known as a scholar of unbending principle.
Start with the sky.
It is a pale ink wash, diluted ink spread broadly to make a grey sky.
The same soft ink, laid on in rounded strokes, describes the pine bark, creating the cold, damp air of a snowy day.
Now the straight pine at the centre, large and commanding.
Its trunk does not waver at all.
Near the top, its branches break off at sharp right angles, giving the picture a vigorous rhythm.
Look at the outlines.
They are drawn with small joints, as if about to break and yet carrying on, and the line itself feels upright and firm.
Dry, scratchy needles and an ink tone with no dark accents give the scene its cold, clear air.
The second pine leans across in front, its roots exposed and its branches reaching out to both sides.
The upright tree and the bent one stand in contrast, setting up a quiet tension across the picture.
Yi In-sang never painted the snow at all.
He left the tops of the rocks and branches as bare paper and laid a pale wash over the sky, so the white seems to settle on its own.
The untouched paper is the snow.
Angular rocks guard the base of the trunk.
The sharp-edged stones below answer the bent branches above, giving this still winter scene both a firm skeleton and a subtle sense of movement.
A scholar who has studied his work describes its character as a restrained beauty that never shows off.
You can feel that restraint here too, in the sparing ink and the generous empty space.
It is a painting that says more by saying less.
A pine that stays evergreen through winter stands for a scholar who keeps his integrity through hardship.
For Yi In-sang, a man of strict principle, this pine was nothing less than a portrait of the very ideal he lived by.
Now step back and take your time with the empty white paper.
In the places where nothing at all is painted, can you see the snow still falling without a sound?
